producedBy.what: One page, put through the GetLoopLoop Vectorscope's fetch, extract and chunk steps locally, with the product's 26-passage cap, and no embedding step. Grouped by the agent's reading, not by embeddings; groups are a judgement, chunking and the 26-passage cap are the product's exact rules.

howToRead.grouping: Grouped by the agent's reading, not by embeddings; groups are a judgement, chunking and the 26-passage cap are the product's exact rules. The product groups passages by average-link clustering over embedding similarity; here the passages were read and grouped by subject instead, so two runs can group the same page differently. For the embedding-based reading with the map, run the page at https://www.getlooploop.com/vectorscope.
howToRead.unitOfAnalysis: A chunk is one passage as the pipeline split it — roughly 2000 characters, following the page's own headings where it has them. Chunks overlap by about 200 characters, so their lengths sum to more than the page.
howToRead.textHead: Only the first 240 characters of each chunk are included. Across this page that is 6053 of 41850 indexed characters, about 14%, and always the opening of each passage rather than a sample spread through it.
howToRead.phrases: Counted over the page's whole text, not the excerpts below. A phrase is two to four content words the page writes side by side — never across a stopword, punctuation or a number — at least twice and in at least two passages (or three times in one), and cohesive enough that the words are not merely neighbours. A shorter phrase nearly always inside a longer one is folded into it. Ranked by `passages` (how many distinct passages use it), then `count`. `groups` is how many of the page's groups it reaches and `describesWholePage` is true when it reaches most of them. These are what the page says, not search demand: nothing here measures how often anybody searches or asks for them. The group counts rest on the grouping above, which is a judgement.
howToRead.narrativeWords: Single words, counted only where none of the listed phrases already used them, so the occurrences still add up. Reporting verbs, connectives and markup residue ([edit] links, TeX) are left out. They say what the page talks about; they are rarely what anybody types or asks.
howToRead.keywords: `phrases` followed by `narrativeWords` as one list, in the shape earlier exports had. Prefer the two lists above.
howToRead.agentLabel: v2: the name the agent gave the group after reading it, or null. It is a judgement, like the grouping; `label` and `labelSource` are the computed label as in v1.
howToRead.groupLabels: `labelSource` says where each name came from. "heading" is the page's own section heading and can be quoted. "keywords" is a computed guess — the group's most distinctive words — and is a hint, not a topic; do not quote it back as what the section is called.
howToRead.cohesion: null: cohesion is the mean cosine between a group's passage embeddings, and no embeddings were computed.
howToRead.selfSimilarity: null: the median cosine between passages needs embeddings, and none were computed.
howToRead.groupFloor: null: there was no similarity cut; the groups are a reading of the passages.
howToRead.duplicateOf: The index of an earlier, non-adjacent chunk this one repeats nearly word for word, as judged by reading — the product judges it from embeddings at cosine 0.94. The chunker's own overlap between neighbours is excluded.
howToRead.projectionExplained: null: there is no projection without vectors.
howToRead.whatCapReachedMeans: The pipeline indexes at most 26 chunks per page. `capReached` true with `charsUnread` above zero means an assistant reading this page never sees that tail.
howToRead.noindex: True when the page asks search engines not to index it. Says nothing about whether an assistant can read it, but it is often unintentional.

cannotAnswer: Sentiment or tone of the page. Only about 14% of the text is here, taken from the opening of each passage — enough to produce a confident-sounding verdict from an unrepresentative sample. If asked, say what the sample supports and that it is a sample.
Anything about competitors, or how this page compares to another. One page was read; no other page was fetched.
Which search or assistant prompts this page ranks or gets cited for. That needs a query inventory and measurement over time, neither of which is in this export.
How often people search for or ask about any phrase listed here. The counts are how often the page says them, not demand.
Whether the page is factually correct, current, or original. Nothing here checked any claim on it.
How the page renders for a browser running JavaScript. This is a plain fetch, which is also what an assistant that does not run JavaScript sees.

How close any two passages are in an embedding space, or whether any assistant has indexed this page. No embeddings were computed, and this is a preview of the machine's view, not a guarantee of what any assistant does with it.
suggestedPrompt: This is a retrieval read-out of one web page. Using it, tell me: (1) what this page is about — lean on `phrases` first, and on those where `describesWholePage` is true most, since they are counted over the full text rather than the excerpts — group by group, naming groups only where labelSource is "heading"; (2) what someone asking an assistant about this subject would find here, and what they would not; (3) what to change first, ordered by how much it would change what an assistant retrieves — cite the chunk indexes or group ids your answer rests on. Where the payload's cannotAnswer list says the data does not support a claim, say so instead of estimating.

plan.problem: The article fills all 26 slots by the middle of "Evaluation"; about 53,000 characters, including Limitations and challenges, Safety and Societal concerns (copyright, energy demands), are never stored.
plan.fix: For a page this long the fix is structural: move the detail of the long middle sections into their "Main article" pages and keep a two-paragraph summary here, so the later sections fall inside the cap.

plan.problem: Every section's text carries the "[ edit ]" link labels; they cost characters in every passage and make "edit" one of the page's top keywords.
plan.fix: Keep edit links out of the readable text (render them as icons with an aria-label, or outside the heading's text node), so the passage starts with the heading's subject.
plan.before: [ edit ] Scaling laws [ edit ] Main article: Neural scaling law
plan.after: Scaling laws. Main article: Neural scaling law

plan.problem: Formulas are extracted twice, as the rendered symbols and as their LaTeX source ("{\displaystyle C}"), so the passages on scaling and perplexity read as noise.
plan.fix: Expose one text form of each formula (the alt text or the MathML, not both), and state the formula's meaning in a sentence next to it.
plan.before: C {\displaystyle C} : cost of pretraining (the total amount of compute used)
plan.after: C: the cost of pretraining a large language model, as the total amount of compute used

plan.problem: Sections such as History run over 2,000 characters under one h2 and are cut by the window, so passages open mid-sentence and lose their subject.
plan.fix: Promote the long sections' subsections to h2, or open each subsection with a sentence that names its subject, so a retriever never receives a passage that starts with a verb.
plan.before: used LSTM-based encoder-decoder architectures, as they preceded the invention of transformers.
plan.after: Early neural machine translation used LSTM-based encoder-decoder architectures, because they preceded the invention of transformers.

plan.problem: Passage #0 is the title twice and nothing else: the page has no meta description for the intro passage to carry.
plan.fix: Add a one-sentence description; the chunker puts it into passage #0.
plan.before: Large language model - Wikipedia Large language model
plan.after: Large language model - Wikipedia. A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on a vast amount of text to generate, summarise, translate and analyse language.

queries.query: what is a large language model

1.quote: A large language model (LLM) is an AI model (typically a neural network) trained on a vast amount of text for natural language processing tasks, especially language generation.
At the 2017 NeurIPS conference, Google researchers introduced the transformer architecture in their landmark paper "Attention Is All You Need".
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is an approach that integrates LLMs with document retrieval systems.

queries.query: how much does it cost to train an LLM

1.quote: the training of GPT-2 (i.e. a 1.5-billion-parameter model) in 2019 cost $50,000, while training of the PaLM (i.e. a 540-billion-parameter model) in 2022 cost $8 million
A 2022 paper demonstrated a separate technique called chain-of-thought prompting, which makes the LLM break the question down autonomously.

queries.query: how is a language model's performance measured

1.quote: The canonical measure of the performance of any language model is its perplexity on a given text corpus.

words.label: Words
words.formula: The extracted body text split on whitespace; every non-empty piece is a word.
words.limits: Counted after the cleaner, so menus, footers and hidden text are not in it. A page drawn by JavaScript reads low here; compare with --render.

headings.label: Headings found
headings.formula: h1 elements plus h2 elements (the first 40) left after the cleaner, with empty ones dropped.
headings.limits: h3 and styled text are not counted: the chunker splits only at h2.

passages.label: Passages read
passages.formula: Sections at h2 headings (or paragraph blocks), long ones cut into 2,000-character windows with about 200 characters of overlap, slivers under 40 characters folded into the passage before, then the first 26 kept.
passages.threshold: At most 26 per page (this tool's cap).
passages.limits: Other systems cut and cap differently; this is a working model of a typical retriever.

slots.label: Cap slots used
slots.formula: Passages kept, out of the 26-passage cap. "Every slot filled" when the chunker produced 26 or more.
slots.threshold: 26: a full cap means text may have been left out (see characters past the cap).
slots.limits: A full cap does not by itself mean text was lost: the last passage may end exactly at the end of the page.

passage_chars.label: Passage length
passage_chars.formula: The length of one passage's text, as the chunker emitted it.
passage_chars.unit: characters, as the passage text holds them
passage_chars.threshold: At most about 2,000, unless a sliver was folded in.
passage_chars.limits: Neighbouring passages share about 200 characters by design.

chars_in_passages.label: Text in passages, overlap and intro included
chars_in_passages.formula: The sum of every passage's length (page.charsIndexed). Passage #0 repeats the title, h1 and meta description; neighbours repeat about 200 characters.
chars_in_passages.unit: characters, as the passage text holds them
chars_in_passages.limits: Counts repeated text more than once, so it can exceed the page's own text. For how much of the page reached a passage, read the unique number.

chars_unique.label: Unique text in passages
chars_unique.formula: Each passage is located in the kept text (the intro part, title, h1 and description, set aside); the union of the located spans is counted once, so overlap is not counted twice.
chars_unique.unit: characters, whitespace runs folded to one space
chars_unique.limits: A passage the locator cannot place is reported as unlocated rather than guessed. Heading lines the chunker carries only as a passage's heading are not in it.

chars_past_cap.label: Characters past the cap
chars_past_cap.formula: Only when every one of the 26 slots is filled: the kept text after the end of the last passage. Equivalently, kept text − unique text in passages − text between passages, counted after the last one.
chars_past_cap.unit: characters, whitespace runs folded to one space
chars_past_cap.threshold: Above 0 means a tail no retriever using this cap can return.
chars_past_cap.limits: Replaces the 2.101 estimate, which subtracted the overlapping total and so undercounted, often to 0. That old number is still exported as charsUnread.

chars_unread_legacy.label: charsUnread (2.101 meaning)
chars_unread_legacy.formula: When the cap is reached: extracted body characters − text in passages including overlap and intro; otherwise 0.
chars_unread_legacy.unit: characters, as the passage text holds them
chars_unread_legacy.limits: Undercounts and can read 0 even when the cap cut a tail. Kept unchanged for compatibility; use characters past the cap.

text_raw.label: Text in the raw HTML
text_raw.formula: Kept text plus every removal in the table below. An estimate of the document's text, defined so the waterfall sums exactly.
text_raw.unit: characters, whitespace runs folded to one space
text_raw.limits: Script and style bodies count as text here because the cleaner has to remove them; it is not the text a reader sees.

text_removed.label: Removed by the cleaner
text_removed.formula: For every element the cleaner removed (outermost only, so nothing counts twice): its own text at the moment of removal. Plus, when a main region was chosen, the text of everything outside it.
text_removed.unit: characters, whitespace runs folded to one space
text_removed.limits: Observed on a second copy of the extraction, checked to give the same text; the removal itself is the product's rule and is not tuned here.

text_kept.label: Kept text
text_kept.formula: The extractor's body text (the chunker's input), whitespace folded.
text_kept.unit: characters, whitespace runs folded to one space
text_kept.limits: Differs slightly from page.bodyChars, which counts line breaks as they are.

not_in_passages.label: Kept, but in no passage text
not_in_passages.formula: Kept text before the end of the last passage that no passage holds: h2 heading lines (carried as a passage's heading, not its text), the spaces between sections, and anything else (should be 0).
not_in_passages.unit: characters, whitespace runs folded to one space
not_in_passages.limits: A retriever may still see a heading as the passage's metadata; this tool does not assume either way.

overlap_chars.label: Overlap
overlap_chars.formula: Located passage text − unique text in passages: what neighbouring windows repeat.
overlap_chars.unit: characters, whitespace runs folded to one space
overlap_chars.limits: By design, about 200 per cut inside a long section.

intro_chars.label: Intro
intro_chars.formula: The title, h1 and meta description the chunker puts at the start of passage #0.
intro_chars.unit: characters, whitespace runs folded to one space
intro_chars.limits: Not part of the body text, so it is outside the waterfall's kept stage.

removal_chars.label: Characters removed by one element
removal_chars.formula: The removed element's text, whitespace folded, at the moment the cleaner removed it.
removal_chars.unit: characters, whitespace runs folded to one space
removal_chars.limits: Elements with no text are counted but not listed. Beyond the first 200 the rest are summed, never dropped.

section_reached.label: Section text that reached a passage
section_reached.formula: For each section the chunker made (the intro, the text before the first h2, each h2), the part of its text inside some passage, over its length.
section_reached.unit: characters, whitespace runs folded to one space
section_reached.threshold: Under 100% means that section lost text, almost always to the cap.
section_reached.limits: When the page has no usable h2 split, the body is one row.

robots_verdict.label: robots.txt verdict
robots_verdict.formula: RFC 9309 over the site's /robots.txt: the group naming the token replaces *; the longest matching Allow or Disallow wins; Allow wins a tie.
robots_verdict.limits: A 4xx robots.txt means no rules; 5xx or no answer means all blocked. Some user-fetch crawlers say they may ignore robots.txt.

markup.label: Technical markup
markup.formula: From the raw HTML: every @type in application/ld+json blocks (through @graph), rel=canonical links, the meta description's length.

render_words.label: Words with JavaScript
render_words.formula: The same extraction and chunking over the DOM a local headless Chrome dumped after running the page's scripts.
render_words.threshold: 50% more words and at least 150 more raises js_dependent.
render_words.limits: Only with --render. The reading itself stays the plain fetch.

group_chars.label: Group size
group_chars.formula: Passages in the group, and the sum of their lengths.
group_chars.unit: characters, as the passage text holds them
group_chars.limits: Computed over the agent's groups, so it moves with the grouping.

group_share.label: Share of indexed text
group_share.formula: The group's characters over the characters of every passage (overlap included).
group_share.limits: Computed over the agent's groups. Overlap counts in both neighbours.

vocabulary.label: Phrase and word counts
vocabulary.formula: Over the passages' text with the overlap removed: ×uses, the passages that use it (p), and how many groups it reaches (g/total).
vocabulary.threshold: A phrase needs 2 uses in 2 passages, or 3 in one.
vocabulary.limits: What the page says, not search demand. The group count rests on the agent's groups.

check_verdicts.label: Check verdicts
check_verdicts.formula: Fixed rules over the measured values, each a named constant in checks.mjs with its reason; every finding names the passages it rests on.
check_verdicts.threshold: Each check's threshold is in the check table of SKILL.md.
check_verdicts.limits: repeated_claim uses the agent's groups; every other check does not.

groups.label: Groups and labels
groups.formula: The agent read every passage and grouped them by subject (at most 6); its label is its own. The label source is computed: a heading most members share, else two distinctive words.
groups.limits: Not an embedding clustering; another model may group a little differently.

duplicates.label: Repeats
duplicates.formula: Passages the agent marked as repeating an earlier, non-adjacent passage almost word for word.
duplicates.limits: The product judges this from embeddings at cosine 0.94; here it is read.

query_verdicts.label: Query test
query_verdicts.formula: For 5 to 10 typical queries, the agent names the best passage and a verdict (complete, partial, missing) and quotes the answer; the quote is checked verbatim.
query_verdicts.limits: Judged from the passages only; it is not a measurement of what any assistant returns.

plan.label: Rewrite plan
plan.formula: The agent's fixes in priority order; each 'before' is checked verbatim against its passage, each cited check against the checks that fired.

facts.label: Citable facts
facts.formula: The agent's list of concrete facts the passages state, each with the passages that state it.
facts.limits: Fact gaps are only as fair as this list is complete.

topic_cells.label: Topic × page cells
topic_cells.formula: Passages and characters of the groups the agent assigned to each shared topic.
topic_cells.unit: characters, as the passage text holds them
topic_cells.limits: Computed over the agent's groups and topics.

diff_counts.label: Changes since the baseline
diff_counts.formula: Passages matched by identical text, then by the same heading in order; the rest are added or removed.
diff_counts.limits: A passage that moved and changed heading counts as removed plus added.

queries.query: what is a large language model

1.quote: A large language model (LLM) is an AI model (typically a neural network) trained on a vast amount of text for natural language processing tasks, especially language generation.
At the 2017 NeurIPS conference, Google researchers introduced the transformer architecture in their landmark paper "Attention Is All You Need".
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is an approach that integrates LLMs with document retrieval systems.

queries.query: how much does it cost to train an LLM

1.quote: the training of GPT-2 (i.e. a 1.5-billion-parameter model) in 2019 cost $50,000, while training of the PaLM (i.e. a 540-billion-parameter model) in 2022 cost $8 million
A 2022 paper demonstrated a separate technique called chain-of-thought prompting, which makes the LLM break the question down autonomously.

queries.query: how is a language model's performance measured

1.quote: The canonical measure of the performance of any language model is its perplexity on a given text corpus.
